fixes.explanation: Right, he stays. Jacob finishes the week's celebration, and Laban gives him Rachel as his wife (Genesis 29:28). Then the text says he worked for Laban another seven years (Genesis 29:30). Nobody packs a bag in this passage, friend. I've been stuck in a place a long time, so I know how a person ends up staying.

Careful, friend, that one is False. When Jacob asks if they know Laban the grandson of Nahor, the shepherds answer, “We know him…” (Genesis 29:5). Then Jacob asks, “Is he well?” and they say, “Yes,” and point out that his daughter Rachel is coming with his sheep (Genesis 29:6). Jacob asked about one man, and he got news and a daughter in the same breath. That's a good return on one question!

He sure does. As soon as Jacob sees Rachel with Laban's sheep, he goes up, rolls the stone away from the mouth of the well, and waters his uncle's sheep (Genesis 29:10). Just before this, the shepherds told him, “We cannot, until all the flocks have been gathered and the stone has been rolled away…” (Genesis 29:8). Then Jacob walks up and rolls it himself. I bet he was thrilled to see her. That stone had been sitting there all day, and he moved it like it owed him money!

Nope, no asking him to wait in this story, friend. Once Jacob tells her he's Rebekah's son and a relative of her father, the text says she ran and told her father (Genesis 29:12). Ran! The only ones waiting at that well were the shepherds, who were waiting for the flocks to gather (Genesis 29:8). If somebody told me a relative of my father was standing at the well, I'd be moving too. I'd trip over my own apron, but I'd be moving.

Duties sound like a job description, but that's not what Laban asks for. He says, "Tell me what your wages should be." (Genesis 29:15) He wants Jacob to name his pay. Duties never paid anybody's bills, friend. A wage is the part where the work gets paid back.

That's Laban's reply. Jacob offers seven years for Rachel, and Laban says, “Better that I give her to you than to another. Stay here with me.” (Genesis 29:19) Notice he doesn't haggle or ask for more. He just says yes and tells Jacob to stay. Fastest deal in the whole passage, and the shortest seven-year contract negotiation ever!

Isaac doesn't come up in Laban's reply. He says, “Better that I give her to you than to another. Stay here with me.” (Genesis 29:19) No asking Dad first here, friend. Laban says it's better to give Rachel to Jacob than to another, and then he tells Jacob to stay.

Isaac's flocks never come up here, friend. Laban says they will give Jacob the younger one in return for another seven years of work (Genesis 29:27). Jacob already spent seven years working for Rachel, so that's a lot of sheep tending to ask for twice. What Laban wants is Jacob's work, and no flocks change hands in this deal.
